tutorial_example_entry.lesson_core_move: Convert a piecewise continuous-time signal into its shifted form by moving each breakpoint in the shift direction and assigning each original formula to the corresponding new interval.

sections.section_title: Introduction to Time Shifts of Piecewise Signals

blocks.text: When a signal is written piecewise, the key thing to recognize is the breakpoint structure. A time shift does not change the formulas themselves; it moves each breakpoint in the shift direction and keeps each formula attached to the corresponding interval.
Use the simplest base case first: a two-piece signal with one breakpoint. Write the original signal so the interval structure is visible before any shift is applied.
For a delay by $T$, the shifted signal is $y(t)=x(t-T)$. That means every breakpoint moves right by $T$, and the same formulas stay attached to the shifted intervals in the same order.

An advance uses the same rule with the breakpoints moved left instead of right. So the real job in every piecewise shift is to move each breakpoint, preserve their order, and rebuild the definition one interval at a time.

example_content.example_prompt: Delay the piecewise constant signal $x(t)=\begin{cases}2,&t<1\\5,&1\le t\end{cases}$ by $T>0$ and write $y(t)=x(t-T)$ as a piecewise definition.

explanation_blocks.text: A delay by $T>0$ means the input time becomes $t-T$. For a piecewise constant signal, the constants do not change; only the breakpoint moves right by $T$.
Here the original breakpoint is at $t=1$, so after the delay it moves to $t=1+T$. The left constant stays on the left of the new breakpoint, and the right constant stays on the right.

So the delayed signal is the same two constants with a shifted breakpoint. That is the pattern to reuse: move the breakpoint, keep the piece values attached to their original sides, and rewrite the intervals in the new order.

example_content.example_prompt: Advance the piecewise constant signal $x(t)=\begin{cases}2,&t<1\\5,&1\le t\end{cases}$ by $T>0$ and write $y(t)=x(t+T)$ as a piecewise definition.

explanation_blocks.text: An advance by $T>0$ means the input time becomes $t+T$. For a piecewise constant signal, the constants do not change; only the breakpoint moves left by $T$.
Here the original breakpoint is at $t=1$, so after the advance it moves to $t=1-T$. The left constant stays on the left of the new breakpoint, and the right constant stays on the right.

So the advanced signal is the same two constants with a shifted breakpoint. That is the pattern to reuse: move the breakpoint left, keep the piece values attached to their original sides, and rewrite the intervals in the new order.

sections.section_title: Shifting Piecewise Formulas That Depend on t

example_content.example_prompt: Delay the piecewise signal $x(t)=\begin{cases}t+2,&t<1\\3-t,&1\le t\end{cases}$ by $T>0$ and write the shifted signal as a piecewise definition.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is that the pieces are formulas in $t$. For this kind of delay, move the breakpoint right by $T$, but do not rewrite the formulas by substituting $t-T$ into them; keep each formula exactly as written on its new interval.
Here the breakpoint at $t=1$ moves to $t=1+T$. The formula $t+2$ stays with the left piece, and the formula $3-t$ stays with the right piece.
So the delayed signal is obtained by translating the interval bounds and reattaching the same formulas. The only change is where each formula lives.

sections.section_title: Shifting a Piecewise Signal with Multiple Breakpoints

example_content.example_prompt: Advance the piecewise signal $x(t)=\begin{cases}1,&t<2\\4,&2\le t<5\\0,&5\le t\end{cases}$ by $T>0$ and write the shifted signal as a piecewise definition.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is that there are two breakpoints, at $t=2$ and $t=5$. Because this is an advance by $T>0$, move both breakpoints left by $T$ and keep each original constant value attached to its interval.
Now rebuild the intervals from left to right. The first piece stays first, the middle piece stays between the shifted breakpoints, and the last piece stays last.
That final form uses each original piece exactly once, with both breakpoints translated in the same direction by the same amount.

sections.section_title: Writing a Complete Shifted Piecewise Definition

example_content.example_prompt: Delay the complete piecewise signal $x(t)=\begin{cases}t+1,&t<0\\3,&0\le t<2\\5-t,&2\le t<4\\1,&4\le t\end{cases}$ by $T>0$ and write the final shifted piecewise definition with all intervals and formulas in order.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is that this is a complete piecewise definition: it has several breakpoints and a mix of constant and $t$-dependent pieces. For a delay by $T>0$, move every breakpoint right by $T$ and keep each formula attached to the same piece.
The breakpoints at $0$, $2$, and $4$ move to $T$, $2+T$, and $4+T$. Rebuild the intervals in order, then reattach the same formulas to the corresponding shifted pieces.
That gives the complete shifted definition with no missing or duplicated pieces.

question_entry.lesson_core_move: Convert a piecewise continuous-time signal into its shifted form by moving each breakpoint in the shift direction and assigning each original formula to the corresponding new interval.

prompt_blocks.text: Delay the piecewise constant signal $x(t)=\begin{cases}4,&t<3\\9,&3\le t\end{cases}$ by $T>0$ and choose the correct piecewise definition for $y(t)=x(t-T)$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: A delay by $T>0$ shifts the breakpoint right by $T$ and keeps the left and right constants on their original sides. So the correct definition is $y(t)=\begin{cases}4,&t<3+T\\9,&3+T\le t\end{cases}$.

prompt_blocks.text: Delay the piecewise constant signal $x(t)=\begin{cases}-1,&t<-2\\6,&-2\le t\end{cases}$ by $T>0$ and choose the correct piecewise definition for $y(t)=x(t-T)$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: A delay by $T>0$ moves the breakpoint right by $T$ and keeps the constants attached to their original intervals. So the delayed signal is $y(t)=\begin{cases}-1,&t<-2+T\\6,&-2+T\le t\end{cases}$.

prompt_blocks.text: Advance the piecewise constant signal $x(t)=\begin{cases}4,&t<2\\-1,&2\le t\end{cases}$ by $T>0$ and choose the correct piecewise definition for $y(t)=x(t+T)$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: An advance uses $y(t)=x(t+T)$, so the breakpoint moves left by $T$ and the constants stay on the same sides.
Choices A, B, C, and D either move the breakpoint the wrong way, fail to shift it, swap the constants, or break the endpoint convention.

prompt_blocks.text: Advance the piecewise constant signal $x(t)=\begin{cases}1,&t<-2\\6,&-2\le t\end{cases}$ by $T>0$ and choose the correct piecewise definition for $y(t)=x(t+T)$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: An advance again means $y(t)=x(t+T)$, so the breakpoint shifts left by $T$ and the values remain attached to their original sides.
Choices A, B, C, and E show the common errors: right shift, no shift, swapped constants, or reversed interval order.

sections.section_title: Shifting Piecewise Formulas That Depend on t

prompt_blocks.text: Delay $x(t)=\begin{cases}t+2,&t<1\\3-t,&1\le t\end{cases}$ by $T>0$. Which piecewise definition is correct for the shifted signal?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Move the breakpoint from $1$ to $1+T$ and keep each formula unchanged. This step is about translating the interval bounds, not substituting $t-T$ into the formulas.

prompt_blocks.text: Delay $x(t)=\begin{cases}2t-1,&t<0\\t^2+1,&0\le t<2\\5-t,&2\le t\end{cases}$ by $T>0$. Which shifted definition is correct?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Shift each breakpoint right by $T$: $0\mapsto T$ and $2\mapsto 2+T$. Keep the formulas $2t-1$, $t^2+1$, and $5-t$ attached to the same left-to-right pieces.

sections.section_title: Shifting a Piecewise Signal with Multiple Breakpoints

prompt_blocks.text: Advance the piecewise signal below by $2$ and choose the correct shifted definition of $y(t)$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: An advance by $2$ moves every breakpoint left by $2$. So $1\mapsto -1$ and $4\mapsto 2$, and the same three constant pieces stay attached to their shifted intervals in order.

That gives $y(t)=\begin{cases}2,&t<-1\\5,&-1\le t<2\\0,&2\le t\end{cases}$. The other choices either shift the breakpoints in the wrong direction, keep one breakpoint fixed, or attach the values to the wrong intervals.

prompt_blocks.text: Advance the piecewise signal below by $2$ and choose the correct shifted definition of $y(t)$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Advance by $2$ means move each breakpoint left by $2$. So $1\mapsto -1$, $3\mapsto 1$, and $6\mapsto 4$, and the original formulas stay in the same left-to-right order.

That gives $y(t)=\begin{cases}1,&t<-1\\-2,&-1\le t<1\\4,&1\le t<4\\0,&4\le t\end{cases}$. The wrong options either shift the breakpoints the wrong way, keep a breakpoint unchanged, reorder the formulas, or drop a piece.

sections.section_title: Writing a Complete Shifted Piecewise Definition

prompt_blocks.text: Delay the piecewise signal below by $T>0$ and choose the correct complete definition of $y(t)$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: A delay by $T$ moves every breakpoint right by $T$ and keeps each formula attached to the same piece.

So the correct shifted definition is $y(t)=\begin{cases}1-t,&t<-2+T\\2,&-2+T\le t<T\\t+1,&T\le t<3+T\\4,&3+T\le t\end{cases}$. The distractors either shift left, leave one bound unchanged, swap formulas, or copy the original intervals.

prompt_blocks.text: Delay the piecewise signal below by $T>0$ and choose the correct complete definition of $y(t)$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: A delay by $T$ shifts the breakpoints from $2$ and $5$ to $2+T$ and $5+T$ while the formulas stay with their original pieces.

So the correct definition is $y(t)=\begin{cases}4,&t<2+T\\t^2,&2+T\le t<5+T\\1-t,&5+T\le t\end{cases}$. The distractors either move the breakpoints left, keep the old bounds, or swap/corrupt the piece order.
